precepts.text: Jacob bought a parcel of a field at Shechem from the children of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money; the field was bought before his sons ever took it by the sword.
precepts.point: Boaz bought all that was Elimelech's, Chilion's and Mahlon's, and purchased Ruth to be his wife to raise up the name of the dead, that it be not cut off from among his brethren.

note.label: The Nativity: the Bloodline, Birthright, & the Messiah

precepts.why:
Genesis 33 gives the history behind the “parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph” in John 4. “Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padan–aram; and pitched his tent before the city. And he bought a parcel of a field, where he had spread his tent, at the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for an hundred pieces of money.”

Jacob bought that land from the Hamites for a hundred pieces of money, and “he erected there an altar, and called it El–elohe–Israel.” A parcel of a field is again the same thing as a parcel of land: an inheritance.

Later, as he was dying, Israel told Joseph, “Moreover I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.” His sons did take the land by the sword; Simeon and Levi went crazy and killed the men of that city. But the field was bought first, before his sons ever took it. So the inheritance at Shechem stood on a lawful purchase, the same way Boaz bought Elimelech's parcel before the elders at the gate.

note.label: Bitterness: The Hidden Leaven From Cain To Esau

precepts.why:
“And Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing wherewith his father blessed him: and Esau said in his heart, The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then will I slay my brother Jacob.” That is the bitterness, and it plans over a process of time. It is the same thing we read in Genesis 4: Cain slew Abel, and Esau wanted to kill Jacob. Cain was the firstborn and Esau was the firstborn. Same spirit.

To see how someone can hold bitterness, hatred and malice toward you and hide it completely, look at Genesis 33, long after Esau said he hated his brother: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.” Someone who hates you can play the long game. He can pretend to be your friend and on your side while he waits for the moment to hit you at your worst. They call them liberals today. That's the liberal for you: oh, we love you niggers, I mean black people. Jacob knew Esau's heart. That is why he sent the gifts ahead: he thought Esau might be coming to kill him.

Hebrews explains what was working in Esau: “Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled”. Looking diligently means looking within yourself. The root of bitterness is a hidden sin under the ground that nobody sees, but over time it springs up and troubles you. It distorts your thoughts and your perception, so that things you once saw clearly, with eyes anointed with eye salve, are no longer pure to you.

“Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” Profane means devoted to what is not sacred, secular rather than religious: Esau was a carnal man, a man of the field, whose religion is sin. When we follow the carnal ways of Esau, we throw away our birthright, the kingdom of heaven. Hebrews says “for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.” Hold on to a bitter spirit and you are a spiritual Edomite, and you will find the same place of no repentance on that day.

An officer drew the parallel: “He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning.” Christ came “that he might destroy the works of the devil”, so we cannot move in the devil's spirit and think we move in Christ's. Whoever does not love his brother is not of God. If there is an offense, deal with it by Matthew 18:15, not by sowing discord in the congregation. “For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace.” The spiritually minded man seeks to gain his brother, not keep him as a rival to get back at, “Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God”.

precepts.text: When a man's ways please the Lord, He maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him; that is what happened with Esau.
precepts.point: The same prayer belongs to us: pray for all that are in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness, keeping the commandments until Christ returns.
precepts.why:
“When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.” That is what happened with Esau.

Jacob bowed himself to the ground seven times as he came near, and Esau “ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.” That embrace is not proof that the hatred was gone. Jacob had prayed for deliverance, and the Most High put that peace on Esau in that moment, because Jacob's ways pleased Him.

precepts.text: Pray for all in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.

precepts.why:
“I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.”

The same prayer belongs to us. Jacob prayed for deliverance, and the Most High made his enemy to be at peace with him in that moment. We pray for all that are in authority, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness, keeping the commandments until Christ returns.

points: That embrace is not proof that the hatred was gone. Jacob had prayed for deliverance, and when a man's ways please the Lord, He maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him; the Most High put that peace on Esau in that moment.
Jacob bowed himself to the ground seven times as he came near, and Esau ran, embraced him, fell on his neck, and kissed him, and they wept.
Jacob presented the children which God graciously gave thy servant, and urged the present on Esau until he took it. Receiving the gift sealed the peace; Jacob wanted the assurance.

Esau offered to travel together and to leave some of his four hundred men, and Jacob declined both, pleading the tender children and the young flocks: I will lead on softly. He stayed wise and kept his distance, and Esau returned that day to Seir.
Jacob journeyed to Succoth, which means booths, built him an house, and made booths for his cattle; the forefather was industrious.
At Shalem he bought a parcel of a field for an hundred pieces of money and erected an altar, and called it Elelohe-Israel: God, the God of Israel.
